"""Conditional-clause openers: "if", "when", "unless" and their equivalents.

The component is layer 15's down_proj component 2688. Its activation is dominated by MLP
hidden unit 2688 of that layer. It is strongly positive on the word that opens a conditional
clause ("If you...", "...only if", "Se", "если", "如果", "wenn"), and near zero on most other
tokens. Sentence-initial "If" is the strongest case. "if" inside code (`if (x)`) is weaker,
and temporal "when" is weaker still. Most of the activation's variance is diffuse and is not
captured by any word list: token identity alone explains only about 7% of it.

The program is stateless. It looks at the current token, and at the token before it to tell
sentence-initial "if" from mid-sentence "if".
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Typical activation when the word is used as a conditional or subordinating opener.
OPENERS = {
    "if": 2.0,
    "unless": 1.5,
    "whenever": 1.8,
    "when": 1.3,
    "suppose": 1.1,
    "once": 0.9,
    "until": 0.8,
    "though": 0.8,
    "whether": 0.7,
    "since": 0.7,
    "because": 0.5,
    "если": 2.3,  # Russian "if"
    "如果": 2.3,  # Chinese "if"
    "wenn": 2.3,  # German "if"
    "si": 2.3,  # Spanish/French/Italian "if"
    "se": 2.3,  # Portuguese "if"
}
SENTENCE_START = {".", "?", "!", ",", ";", ":", "(", "-", '"', "\n"}
SENTENCE_IF = 3.1  # "If" opening a sentence or clause


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    value = OPENERS.get(word, 0.0)
    if word == "if" and len(prefix.token_strings) > 1:
        if prefix.token_strings[-2].strip() in SENTENCE_START:
            value = SENTENCE_IF
    return carry, float(value)

"""Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:2691 (layer 15 MLP output, one rank-one piece).

What the component is: its input reads mostly MLP hidden unit 2691 of layer 15, and its
direct effect on the output promotes null-like value words (NULL, null, ZERO, nil, empty,
nullptr) while suppressing unrelated foreign-word tokens. It is most often positive right
after an equals sign, an "is", or a colon, where a value may follow ("x = ", "is ", "... to ").
Its activation is mostly small, diffuse, context-driven noise (about -0.04 typically), with
occasional large positive spikes (up to ~10); the spikes have no simple prefix rule that we found.

What this program does: it predicts the component's mean level, shifted up on tokens that
introduce a value (=, ==, :, is, be, are, was, to, equal, equals), and predicts 0 at the first
token of each document, where the component is silent. It reads only the newest token and the
document labels. It captures the tendency but not the spikes or the diffuse fluctuation: on the
training sample it explains well under 1% of the variance.

Values are the means measured on 8192 training rows: about 0.08 after a value-introducing token,
about -0.04 elsewhere, and about 0 at a document's first token.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

VALUE_INTRODUCERS = {"=", "==", ":", "is", "be", "are", "was", "to", "equal", "equals"}
MEAN_AFTER_INTRODUCER = 0.08
MEAN_ELSEWHERE = -0.04


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    t = prefix.position
    if t == 0 or prefix.document_ids[t] != prefix.document_ids[t - 1]:
        return carry, 0.0
    word = prefix.token_strings[t].strip()
    if word in VALUE_INTRODUCERS:
        return carry, MEAN_AFTER_INTRODUCER
    return carry, MEAN_ELSEWHERE

"""Obligation / necessity detector (v3).

The component is negative where the text is about to state something that is required,
needed or recommended: at the word just before a bare verb of obligation ("must", "should",
"need to", "have to", "encouraged to", "unless", "please"). Positions are near zero otherwise.
"""
READS = ()

OBLIGATION = {  # modal and deontic words, in English and a few other languages
    "must": -4.3, "Must": -5.5, "MUST": -6.0, "should": -2.8, "ought": -3.3,
    "need": -2.5, "needs": -2.5, "require": -3.5, "required": -3.5, "requires": -3.5,
    "Required": -4.0, "requiring": -4.0, "mandatory": -3.3, "prohibited": -3.0,
    "recommend": -4.0, "recommends": -4.5, "recommended": -3.0, "encourage": -5.0,
    "encourages": -5.0, "encouraged": -6.0, "urging": -4.5, "please": -3.5,
    "Please": -3.5, "unless": -5.0, "necessary": -1.3, "essential": -1.3,
    "sure": -2.0, "important": -2.0, "welcome": -3.5, "want": -2.0, "wants": -2.5,
    "hope": -2.0, "ensure": -1.7, "supposed": -2.9, "preferably": -3.2,
    "必须": -5.0, "需要": -2.2, "请": -2.8, "欢迎": -10.0, "禁止": -5.6, "不要": -2.9,
    "необходимо": -5.3, "нужно": -4.2, "должен": -5.1, "должна": -5.5, "должны": -4.8,
    "debe": -5.0, "deben": -4.9, "deve": -4.8, "doit": -4.2, "faut": -3.9, "muss": -4.9,
}
# Modals and infinitive-taking words: a weak negative lean toward a following bare verb.
WEAK = {"can": -0.6, "may": -0.7, "could": -0.5, "cannot": -1.4, "might": -0.4,
        "be": -0.7, "been": -0.4, "being": -0.6, "if": -1.2, "for": -0.5, "that": -0.3,
        "any": -0.6, "only": -0.6, "until": -1.1, "keep": -1.1, "get": -0.6}
# Words after which "to" is an obligation infinitive ("have to", "asked to", "told to").
TO_AFTER_OBLIGATION = {
    "have", "has", "had", "need", "needs", "required", "require", "requires", "encouraged",
    "encourage", "asked", "told", "instructed", "supposed", "forced", "allowed", "free",
    "expected", "invited", "you", "us", "them", "me", "him", "her",
}
MODAL_BEFORE_BE = {"must", "should", "to", "can", "may", "need"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    cur = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    same_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip() if same_doc else ""
    if cur == "to":
        return carry, (-4.0 if prev in TO_AFTER_OBLIGATION else -0.6)
    if cur == "be":
        return carry, (-1.2 if prev in MODAL_BEFORE_BE else -0.4)
    if cur in OBLIGATION:
        return carry, OBLIGATION[cur]
    return carry, WEAK.get(cur, 0.0)

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 2693: predicts (almost) nothing.

What the component is: a rank-one piece of the MLP down projection that reads the
layer-15 MLP hidden vector h and adds (h . V) * |U| to the residual stream. Its
readout vector is about 0.69 in norm, and 0.38 of that norm sits on the hidden unit
2693 itself; the rest is spread thinly over thousands of hidden units.

What we measured (on training rows and the eval rows):
- Its activation has mean ~0 and std ~0.30, and it is positive in ~95% of its
  large (|a| > 1.5) cases. Chat-template and assistant-reply contexts are enriched
  among the large values (about 13% of them, against under 1% of all tokens), but
  they are too few to matter for variance.
- No surface feature explains it: the token identity, the character class of the
  token, whether the token or bigram was seen earlier in the row, the position in
  the document, and an exponentially decaying history of token classes all give
  held-out variance explained below 0.002.
- Its logit-lens direction (U times the tied embedding) promotes and suppresses
  unrelated tokens, so it has no readable output role.
- It almost never passes the causal-importance threshold (0 of 10M tokens) and
  switching it off changes the model's next-token predictions by about 1e-6 nats.

So this program predicts the mean, 0, at every position. That is the honest
description: there is no concept here that a token-level program can state.
"""

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Predict the component's activation at this position: always 0."""
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 2695: a "things vary / change / stay fixed" feature.

In plain terms: this component leans positive while the text is about something that
varies, is adjustable, or stays fixed or constant ("adjustable", "varying", "fixed",
"constant", "always", "changing the ..."). The push is strongest on the adjectives
of that kind, weaker on the verbs and nouns ("vary", "variation", "depend"), and it
carries a little way past the word, fading with distance. It is near zero in most
other text, and some code, markup and boilerplate sit slightly below zero, which
this program does not model.

The program keeps a score per document. Each token adds its weight if it is a
variation word (STRONG_WORDS adds 1.0, WEAK_WORDS adds WEAK), and the score fades by
DECAY at each later token. A new document resets the score. The prediction is
SCALE * score + BASE, where BASE is the component's typical resting value.

This explains only a little of the variance (about 0.3 to 0.4% on sampled
training text, and on eval): the component's spread is diffuse, and no word list
or bag of preceding words explains more than about 1%.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

STRONG_WORDS = frozenset(
    """
    adjustable varying persistent fixed movable removable portable adaptive flexible
    stable versatile universal constant consistently changing responsive uniform
    invariant volatile variable always
    """.split()
)

WEAK_WORDS = frozenset(
    """
    vary varies varied variation variations variability change changes alter modify
    adjust adjusting adjustment maintain maintaining maintains depend depends dependent
    dependence dependency constantly consistent stability fix variant variables
    """.split()
)

WEAK = 0.3  # a weak word's weight, against 1.0 for a strong one
DECAY = 0.6  # how much of the score survives each token
SCALE = 0.7  # activation per unit of score
BASE = 0.02  # the component's typical resting value


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    score = 0.0 if carry is None else carry
    if prefix.position > 0 and prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        score = 0.0  # a new document starts: forget the earlier text
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    weight = 1.0 if word in STRONG_WORDS else WEAK if word in WEAK_WORDS else 0.0
    score = DECAY * score + weight
    return score, SCALE * score + BASE

"""Component 2696 of layer 15's MLP down_proj (Qwen3-1.7B).

Its activation is almost entirely a read of MLP hidden unit 2696 at layer 15 (about a
third of its variance) plus many small weights. It is a diffuse, weakly lexical signal.
The word-level pattern that does exist is a sign split between REMOVAL and NEGATION:

- Removal verbs (remove, eliminate, discard, delete, rm, vanish, clear, kill, reject,
  reduce, subtract, erase) go strongly negative when used as an action, i.e. after a cue
  that introduces a verb (to, can, will, you, we, and, a comma). Used as nouns or after
  "a"/"the", they stay near zero.
- The minus sign " -" (subtraction) leans slightly negative, the same direction.
- Negation and absence words (not, n't, no, non-, without, unable, never, less) go
  positive, more so after a modal or auxiliary (may, would, should, don, did, do).
- Everything else sits near the component's mean, about 0.04.

Predicting these classes explains only a small share of the variance; the rest is not
carried by word identity or by the words nearby.
"""

READS = ()

REMOVAL = {" remove", " removing", " removes", " removed", " eliminate", " eliminating",
           " discard", " delete", " rm", " vanish", " clear", " kill", " reject", " reduce",
           " subtract", " erase"}
CUE = {" to", " can", " will", " you", " we", " and", ",", " must", " should"}
NEGATION = {" not", "'t", "’t", " no", " non", " without", " unable", " never", " less"}
AUX = {" may", " would", " should", " don", " do", " did", " does", " will", " can",
       " was", " is"}
MINUS = {" -"}

REMOVAL_AFTER_CUE, REMOVAL_OTHER = -1.3, -0.6
NEGATION_AFTER_AUX, NEGATION_OTHER = 0.4, 0.25
MINUS_VALUE = -0.25
BASE = 0.04


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Activation at the newest token, from its word and the word before it."""
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    same_doc = len(prefix.token_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2] if same_doc else ""
    if word in REMOVAL:
        value = REMOVAL_AFTER_CUE if before in CUE else REMOVAL_OTHER
    elif word in NEGATION:
        value = NEGATION_AFTER_AUX if before in AUX else NEGATION_OTHER
    elif word in MINUS:
        value = MINUS_VALUE
    else:
        value = BASE
    return carry, float(value)


def main():
    """Print the program's value at each token of a short sentence."""
    words = [" we", " can", " remove", " the", " old", " file", " not", " used"]
    carry = None
    for i, word in enumerate(words):
        carry, value = step(carry, _Demo(words[: i + 1]), {})
        print(repr(word), value)


class _Demo:
    """A one-document stand-in for the scorer's prefix, for the demo above."""

    def __init__(self, words):
        self.token_strings = words
        self.token_ids = list(range(len(words)))
        self.document_ids = [0] * len(words)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Command detector for layers.15.mlp.down_proj, unit 2697.

The unit is positive inside an instruction written to the reader in ordinary
prose: on the command verb that opens it ("Click the link", "Join us",
"Review the changes", "Think of ..."), on the word "please", and on the words
that follow inside the same command (the object, a particle such as "up" or
"out", a conjoined verb after "and"), fading as the command goes on. It is
near zero in narration and reasoning, in code, and when the verb sits in the
middle of a clause ("you can make", "to make").

The program keeps one number, the command's strength, carried from token to
token:
- a command verb that opens a sentence (or follows "please", "then" or "just")
  sets the strength to 1;
- each later token in the same sentence multiplies it by DECAY;
- a full stop, question mark, exclamation mark or newline ends the command.
The prediction is ONSET times the strength, plus PLEASE on the word "please".

What this leaves out: commands in other languages, verbs not in the list,
and the weak negative on sentence-initial "You"/"Your". The list is English
bare-form verbs of instruction, not every verb, so the score is modest
(variance explained about 0.04 to 0.05 on training rows).
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

COMMAND_VERBS = frozenset(
    """add answer apply ask assume avoid be become beware book bring buy
    calculate call check choose click come compare complete connect
    consider contact continue create define describe determine discover do
    download draw edit enjoy ensure enter explain explore fill find follow
    forget generate get give grab have help hold imagine implement impress
    include join keep learn leave listen look make note notice open pay
    pick place plan play practice prepare press protect rate read receive
    relax remember reply report review save say see select share show sit
    start stay study subscribe support take talk tell think throw try turn
    understand upgrade use visit watch write""".split()
)
"""Bare-form verbs that give orders to a reader, as in "Take a break" or
"Subscribe now". Code and reasoning verbs (print, return, test, let, wait) and
verbs that are rarely imperative in prose are left out."""

LEADS_IN = frozenset({"please", "then", "just"})
"""Words after which a command verb still opens a command: "Please subscribe"."""

SENTENCE_END = ".!?\n"
ONSET = 3.4
"""Prediction for a command at full strength (its verb)."""
DECAY = 0.5
"""Fraction of the command's strength left one token later."""
PLEASE = 4.1
"""Extra prediction on the word "please" itself."""


def _word(token: str) -> str:
    return token.strip().lower()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    tokens = prefix.token_strings
    position = prefix.position
    new_document = position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    if carry is None or new_document:
        strength, last_word, at_sentence_start = 0.0, "", True
    else:
        strength, last_word, at_sentence_start = carry

    word = _word(tokens[-1])
    strength *= DECAY
    if word.isalpha() and word in COMMAND_VERBS and (at_sentence_start or last_word in LEADS_IN):
        strength = 1.0
    value = ONSET * strength + (PLEASE if word == "please" else 0.0)

    ends_sentence = any(c in tokens[-1] for c in SENTENCE_END)
    if ends_sentence:
        strength = 0.0
    if word.isalpha():
        last_word = word
    at_sentence_start = ends_sentence or tokens[-1].strip() == ""
    return (strength, last_word, at_sentence_start), float(value)

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 2698: a near-constant predictor.

What the component is: a rank-one piece of the MLP's down projection. Its read
direction is dominated by one hidden unit, neuron 2698 of layer 15's MLP (read weight
0.50; the next-largest weight is 0.07). Its activation correlates 0.52 with that hidden
unit's value (about 27% of its variance), so the rest comes from many small weights.
The hidden unit is dense and context-dependent: its value has no clear token, position,
or repetition signature that a short program can name (see the explanation).

What this program does: it predicts exactly 0 at the first token of every document
(where the component's activation is always exactly 0 in the data), and the average
activation, about 0.02, everywhere else. It does not model the context-dependent
variation, which is most of the signal.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.02


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    n = len(prefix.document_ids)
    first_of_document = n == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    return carry, 0.0 if first_of_document else MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15, MLP hidden unit 2699 (down_proj component 2699): a weak time-span detector.

This component is almost exactly one MLP neuron: its input direction is that unit
(weight 0.87 of norm 1.07), so its activation is that neuron's SwiGLU value times
about 0.96. The neuron's activation is diffuse and mostly unpredictable from the text. The one
concept that leans its way is time span: on words that name or continue a stretch of
time ("years", "during", "since", "always", "over"), it averages clearly negative.
Everywhere else it sits near its overall average, a little above zero. The program
predicts the span value on those words and the average elsewhere. It explains very
little of the variance; most of the activation is spikes no word list captures.
"""

READS = ()

TIME_SPAN_WORDS = frozenset({
    "year", "years", "during", "since", "always", "ever", "over", "until",
    "continue", "continued", "continues", "continuing", "continuously",
    "constant", "constantly", "time", "times", "period", "decades", "months", "days",
})
SPAN_VALUE = -0.11
OTHER_VALUE = 0.026


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    return carry, SPAN_VALUE if word in TIME_SPAN_WORDS else OTHER_VALUE

"""layers.15.mlp.down_proj:2700, a weak English-adjective proxy.

This component is almost entirely MLP hidden unit 2700 of layer 15 (its input vector has
0.76 of its norm on that unit). Its value is dense, around 0 with std 0.44, and it changes
the model's output very little. Almost none of its variance is explained by readable
features we tested: the token identity explains about 3% out of sample, and the words before
it explain nothing.

The one lexical tendency we found is that English adjectives (by WordNet) are slightly more
variable and lean negative on average, although about half of them are positive. This program
predicts a small negative value on each English adjective and 0 on every other token.
"""

from functools import lru_cache

import regex
import wordnet

READS = ()

ADJECTIVE_VALUE = -0.024
"""The predicted activation on an English adjective: the training sample's mean there (-0.024)."""


@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def is_english_adjective(token: str) -> bool:
    """True for a bare lowercase English word that WordNet lists as an adjective."""
    word = token.strip().lower()
    return bool(regex.fullmatch(r"[a-z]+", word)) and "adjective" in wordnet.parts_of_speech(word)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Predict the value at the newest token: a small negative on English adjectives, else 0."""
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    return carry, ADJECTIVE_VALUE if is_english_adjective(token) else 0.0

"""Scarcity / demand / congestion topic detector for layers.15.mlp.down_proj:2701.

What the component responds to: it is quiet on most text, but stays active through
passages about things being in short supply or crowded: "sold out", "in stock",
"demand", "supply", "shortage", "limited capacity", "busy", "traffic jam",
"waiting", "queue", and their Chinese equivalents. Its output direction promotes words
such as "busy", "crowded", "shortage", "scarce" and "queue", so it helps the model
expect that kind of word next.

This program keeps a running topic score that decays with distance: each token adds 1
if it is a topic word, and the score fades by a factor DECAY per token. The
prediction is a small baseline plus a scaled score. The score resets at each document
boundary, as the model's attention does.
"""

READS = ()

TOPIC_WORDS = (
    # English: supply and demand, stock, capacity, congestion, waiting
    "demand", "supply", "shortage", "lack", "scarc", "capacity", "stock",
    "sold", "traffic", "congest", "jam", "queue", "busy", "crowd", "overload",
    "availab", "limited", "wait", "rush",
    # Chinese: demand, stock, sold out, traffic, queue, quota, scarce, busy
    "需求", "供", "库存", "售", "流量", "拥", "排队", "名额", "限", "缺", "抢",
    "紧张", "繁忙", "堵", "热门", "等待",
)
DECAY = 0.85  # how much of the score survives one more token
SCALE = 0.41  # activation per unit of topic score (least-squares fit)
BASELINE = -0.056  # the component's typical value away from any topic


def is_topic(token_string):
    text = token_string.lower()
    return any(word in text for word in TOPIC_WORDS)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    score, doc = carry if carry is not None else (0.0, None)
    document = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if document != doc:
        score = 0.0  # a new document starts: forget the old topic
    score = DECAY * score + (1.0 if is_topic(prefix.token_strings[-1]) else 0.0)
    return (score, document), BASELINE + SCALE * score

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 2702: a near-constant predictor.

What the component is: a rank-one piece of the layer-15 MLP's down projection. Its
input is almost entirely MLP hidden unit 2702 (about 0.48 of its read direction), and its
output direction writes into the residual stream with norm 0.89. Its activation is a
small, dense, noise-like signal (std 0.38, mean 0.06) with no simple description we
could find: it is not set by the current token's identity or class (token identity
explains under 3% of its variance even with a 100k-entry lookup table), nor by the
next-token loss, the prediction entropy, the residual norm, or the repeated-token
pattern. Its one structural feature is at document starts: the first token of a
document gives about 0, and the second token gives a little more than the rest.

So this program predicts the average level everywhere, with the document-start rule:
0 at the first token of each document, 0.13 at the second, 0.06 elsewhere. It reads
only the token positions, not the tokens' content, and carries the position in its
document in `carry`. It explains close to none of the variance (its value is about 0
on held-out data), and it does not describe what the component responds to.
"""

READS = ()

FIRST_TOKEN = 0.0  # the first token of a document: the component is silent there
SECOND_TOKEN = 0.13  # the second token of a document
ELSEWHERE = 0.06  # the average activation at all other positions


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        index = 0  # the first token of a new document (or of the row)
    else:
        index = carry[1] + 1
    if index == 0:
        value = FIRST_TOKEN
    elif index == 1:
        value = SECOND_TOKEN
    else:
        value = ELSEWHERE
    return (doc, index), value

"""Layer 15, MLP unit 2703 (down_proj component 2703) as a concession detector.

This component's activation is almost entirely one MLP hidden unit (its input
direction is about two-thirds that single unit). It goes clearly negative where the
text has just turned to a contrast or concession: on "but", "however", "yet",
"though", "still", "nevertheless", "despite" (and their Chinese and Japanese
equivalents), and on the first few words of the clause that follows, before the
sentence ends. Its negative output promotes continuations such as "nevertheless",
"anyway", "nonetheless", so it is part of how the model carries a concession forward.

This program says just that: a constant negative value on a contrast word, a
weaker one on the next three tokens of the same sentence, and zero elsewhere.
It gets the sign and place of the strongest negatives, but not their size. Most of
the variance is in small values this sketch does not describe.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Words that set up a contrast or concession.
CONTRAST = {
    " but", " But", "but", "But", " however", " However", "however",
    " yet", " Yet", " though", " Though", " although", " Although",
    " still", " Still", " nevertheless", " Nevertheless", " despite", " Despite",
    "但", "但是", "可是", "然而", "不过", "でも", "けど", "しかし",
}  # fmt: skip

# Tokens that end a sentence, closing any open concession.
SENTENCE_END = {".", "!", "?", "\n", ".\n", "\n\n", "。", "！", "？"}

WINDOW = 3  # tokens after a contrast word that carry a weaker negative value
